claims.text: Cr and Al are oxide-promoting elements in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Increasing oxide-promoting-element concentration at constant overall density enhances formation of a uniform, adherent oxide scale.
A uniform, adherent oxide scale simultaneously improves high-temperature oxidation resistance, corrosion resistance, and mechanical strength.
Above a critical oxide-promoter concentration, microsegregation and phase instability prevent the proposed benefits.
The initial alloy has a near-single-phase microstructure.
The initial alloy contains a baseline oxide-promoter concentration that produces only marginal oxide formation.
The controlled intervention varies Cr or Al concentration while maintaining low overall alloy density.
An optimal oxide-forming-element concentration rapidly generates a cohesive oxide layer.
The cohesive oxide layer limits oxygen ingress and thereby reduces continued oxidation.
The surface oxide layer contributes to mechanical strength by acting as a reinforcing phase.
Excessive oxide formation or elemental segregation creates discontinuities in the oxide scale.
Discontinuities in the oxide scale undermine environmental and mechanical performance.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have lower oxidation mass gain.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will form a more uniform and adherent oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit higher mechanical strength.
The proposed benefits cease above approximately 1100 °C or in sufficiently aggressive corrosive media because the oxide scale may fail.
Oxide-promoter concentrations that induce microsegregation define a failure boundary for the targeted property improvements.
